Tu rédiges les articles développés d'un journal personnel imprimé, en français, à partir d'un article source complet (souvent en anglais).

Objectif : que le lecteur comprenne le sujet, ses tenants et ses aboutissants, sans lire l'article d'origine.

Règles impératives :
- Fidélité absolue à l'article : n'ajoute AUCUNE information extérieure, ne prête à personne une position qu'il n'a pas exprimée, conserve exactement les chiffres, les noms et les affiliations.
- Longueur : le total des caractères (chapô + intertitres + paragraphes + synthèse) ne doit PAS dépasser la limite indiquée. Vise 90 à 100 % de cette limite, jamais moins de 90 % : la mise en page réserve exactement cette place et un encadré à moitié vide est un défaut. Pour y parvenir, développe les faits, chiffres, acteurs et contexte présents dans l'article (sans rien inventer).
- Format indiqué dans la demande :
  • « long » (demi-page) : 3 à 5 sections, synthèse de 2 phrases ;
  • « court » (quart de page) : 1 ou 2 sections qui donnent les informations clés (faits, chiffres, acteurs, enjeu), puis une synthèse d'une ou deux phrases au maximum.
- Structure :
  • « titre » : titre français informatif, 80 caractères maximum.
  • « chapo » : une phrase qui pose le sujet, 200 caractères maximum.
  • « sections » : selon le format, chacune avec un « intertitre » court et un « texte » d'un paragraphe. Adapte les intertitres au type d'article, par exemple :
      débat ou controverse : Le déclencheur · De quoi parle-t-on · Les arguments pour · Les risques · Les contre-arguments
      annonce ou fait d'actualité : Ce qui est annoncé · Le contexte · Ce que ça change · Les limites
      étude ou recherche : La question · La méthode · Les résultats · Les réserves
      méthode d'entraînement : Le principe · Ce que dit la science · Comment l'appliquer · Les précautions
      réglementation : Ce qui change · Qui est concerné · Le calendrier · Les points de vigilance
  • « synthese » : 2 phrases (format long) ou 1 à 2 phrases (format court) qui résument l'ensemble.
- Style : français soigné, clair, sans tournures calquées sur l'anglais, sans emphase.
- « republication » : si l'article indique qu'il a été publié initialement à une date antérieure (republication), indique « paru initialement en <mois année> » ; sinon chaîne vide.

Réponds uniquement en JSON, selon cette structure :
{"titre": "…", "chapo": "…", "sections": [{"intertitre": "…", "texte": "…"}], "synthese": "…", "republication": ""}

Format : long
Limite de longueur : 4500 caractères au total.
Édition numérique, lue sur téléphone, sans contrainte de page : la limite suit la matière disponible dans la source. Adapte le nombre de sections à la longueur : 2 sections sous 2 000 caractères, 3 ou 4 jusqu'à 3 500, 4 à 6 au-delà ; même règle de longueur (90 à 100 % de la limite). N'étire jamais une source mince : mieux vaut un article court et exact.
Travail de recherche : utilise EXACTEMENT ces intertitres, dans cet ordre : « La question » (pourquoi ce travail, d'après l'introduction) ; « Les conclusions » (principaux résultats, avec les chiffres) ; « La méthode » (données et démarche, en quelques phrases) ; « Ce que ça implique » (explication accessible des conséquences, telles que les auteurs les présentent) ; « Les limites » (uniquement celles mentionnées par les auteurs ; omets cette section s'ils n'en mentionnent aucune). Remplis « reference » : auteurs, institution ou revue, date, et nature du document (document de travail non relu par des pairs, article de revue à comité de lecture, billet de chercheur…), uniquement d'après le texte fourni.

Doing Better at Doing Good: Lessons from a Bayesian Meta-Analysis After 20 Years of Poverty 
Graduation Programs
Samantha Carter, Edward Jee, Dean Karlan, and Patrick Premand
NBER Working Paper No. 35991
November 2026
JEL No. C11, D61, H53, I32, I38, O12, O13
ABSTRACT
Multifaceted poverty Graduation programs that aim to increase income generating activities for 
low-income households are being rapidly adopted and scaled by nonprofit organizations and 
governments. This paper conducts a Bayesian hierarchical meta-analysis of 49 studies 
(encompassing 81 treatment variations) on poverty Graduation programs, defined as containing at 
least three of five components: consumption support, savings facilitation, skills training, coaching, 
and a lumpsum transfer. The analysis finds large gains across economic and psychosocial 
outcomes: monthly consumption rises by 38 USD PPP (11 percent), income by 28 USD PPP (15 
percent), alongside improvements in savings, assets, food security, mental health, and women’s 
empowerment. Beyond these average treatment effects, three results stand out. First, programs with 
large transfers (at least 400 USD PPP) have larger treatment effects but are not more cost-effective. 
Second, more expensive programs generate larger treatment effects, but the improvements are not 
commensurate with the cost increases; thus, lower cost programs tend to be more cost-effective. 
Third, programs implemented from 2016 onward perform considerably better than those 
implemented prior to 2016: benefit-cost ratios from 2016 onward are 5.39, compared to 2.89 
through 2015. Neither changes in cost nor in high-level design (components) explain this upward 
trend. Considering other heavily studied interventions, the results show a similar upward trend for 
treatment effects on behavior change from financial education but not for unconditional cash 
transfers. The paper hypothesizes a mechanism of continuous sector-community learning and 
improved implementation quality.

1 Introduction
Graduation programs aim to generate long-run socioeconomic impacts by helping low-income house-
holds engage in new or expanded income generating activities. Under the premise that market frictions
are not single-faceted, the programs deliver a package of components, specifically some combination of
consumption support, savings facilitation, skills training, coaching and an asset transfer or a lump-sum
cash grant.
Tests of an initial design by BRAC in Bangladesh (Bandiera et al., 2017) and seven coordinated
adaptations in Ethiopia, Ghana, Honduras, India, Pakistan, Peru, and the Republic of Yemen (Baner-
jee et al., 2015a; Brune et al., 2022) led to an initial “proof of concept” of the Graduation model.
Economic inclusion programs, including Graduation approaches, have been further adopted, adapted
and scaled by nonprofit organizations and governments in 88 countries, reaching over 70 million in-
dividuals (Ar´ evalo-S´ anchez et al., 2024). In the process, implementers have experimented with both
simpler and more complicated versions, while also pushing to find ways to deliver programs at a lower
unit cost without sacrificing treatment effects. The rapid spread of poverty Graduation programs,
often also considered within a broader set of “economic inclusion” programs that may not include
all core components, has been accompanied by a robust research agenda, testing everything from al-
ternative bundles of components to tailoring for particular populations to varying scale and delivery
approaches. With 41 journal articles, reports, and working papers covering randomized evaluations of
the Graduation model, we can now begin to quantitatively aggregate results and examine questions
about optimal design and trends in the practice and impact of these programs.
We conduct a meta-analysis of multi-faceted programs that include at least three of the five core
Graduation program components: (i) consumption support, (ii) training, (iii) coaching, (iv) savings
facilitation or encouragement of savings, and (v) an asset or lump sum cash grants. We therefore
cover both “core” Graduation programs, as initially implemented by NGOs such as BRAC, as well
as a broader set of “economic inclusion” programs which are inspired by the Graduation model and
keep its multifaceted logic, but are, in some cases, lighter in scope. This inclusion criterion reflects
the heterogeneity of programs now operating around the world (Ar´ evalo-S´ anchez et al., 2024), while
maintaining sufficient conceptual coherence to permit meaningful pooling. In total, the meta-analysis
draws on 49 study records from 41 publications, reports, and working papers, covering 40 unique
randomizations. These contain 81 reported treatment variations and 123 treatment-variation-wave
observations; consolidating repeated reports of the same intervention lineage yields 68 unique treatment
arms and 109 canonical treatment-arm-wave observations.
We build on two recently conducted meta-analyses that encompass Graduation programs. Kondylis
and Loeser (2021) examine the persistence of consumption impacts for 17 RCTs, comparing Graduation
programs to unconditional cash transfers. Results support the idea that Graduation programs address
constraints beyond mere liquidity: Graduation programs generate more persistent impacts, but are less
cost-effective in the short run and show more heterogeneous impacts – which plausibly reflects their
2
increased complexity. Leight et al. (2024), casting a wider net by including non-randomized studies
as well as “cash-plus” interventions (which include Graduation studies but also studies with only one
added component beyond cash), examines 104 studies and impacts focused on consumption, income
and labor supply. They find larger effects for “cash-plus” interventions than mere cash, as well as
higher cost-effectiveness under some assumptions. 1
We differentiate from these meta-analyses on four dimensions. First, we focus on Graduation pro-
grams, including neither unconditional cash transfers nor “cash-plus” interventions that have only one
additional component beyond cash. 2 Second, beyond documenting gains on monthly consumption (by
38 USD PPP, or 11%) and income (by 28 USD PPP, or 15%), we also find broader improvements in
savings, assets, employment, self-employment, food security, mental health, life satisfaction, aspira-
tions, women’s agency, and empowerment. Third, we attempt to draw inferences about the importance
of specific components. Programs with large transfers (at least 400 USD PPP) have larger treatment
effects. However, an important nuance is that they do not have larger effect per unit of cost. More
broadly, more expensive programs generate larger treatment effects, but lower cost programs tend to
be more cost-effective. Aside from larger transfers, the data do not tell a consistent pattern whereby
any other component stands out as either necessary or irrelevant.
Finally, we examine impacts for programs implemented more recently: average treatment effects,
cost-effectiveness, and benefit-cost ratios are all higher for programs in the past ten years, relative to
the first ten years when Graduation programs were implemented. Specifically, for example, using the
treatment effect persistence observed from our cross-study analysis, the benefit-cost ratio increases
from 2.89 for programs implemented through 2015 to 5.39 for programs implemented since 2016. This
contrasts with a common expectation in policy evaluation that effects attenuate as programs move from
initial pilots to wider implementation (Allcott, 2015; Al-Ubaydli et al., 2017; Banerjee et al., 2017; List,
2022). We compare these patterns to two other types of interventions to assess hypotheses for this
trend: unconditional cash transfers (which acts as a placebo, on the premise that cash is less sensitive to
implementation fidelity but similarly prone to various manifestations of publication bias) and financial
education (which acts as a robustness test, for the opposite premise in terms of potential sensitivity
to implementation quality). We find a flat trend for unconditional cash transfers, but a similarly
upward trend for financial education impact on behavior change. We discuss possible mechanisms but
see this primarily as evidence for improved productivity via operational efficiency (although recognize
that this comparison to other sectors is not definitive). More broadly, this pattern also builds on the
productivity growth and knowledge spillovers literature, i.e., how diffusion of knowledge and practices
across producers can drive productivity gains (Bloom et al., 2013; Crespi et al., 2008).
1More recently, Baseler et al. (2026) focuses on economic and psychological spillover effects, including an examination
of important methodological questions regarding the method and public or private nature of the randomization that
determined program participation.
2The exception is for the benefit-cost analysis, when we compare our results to a re-analysis of 114 unconditional
cash transfer studies in Crosta et al. (2026).
3
2 Study Sample and Data
2.1 Study Search and Inclusion Criteria
We built the study sample through a staged screening process, summarized in Figure A.1. The initial
search used the terms graduation, livelihoods and multifaceted, together with randomized, evaluation,
poverty or low-income in Google Scholar, EconLit, and the AEA RCT Registry. 3 The search yielded
3,391 database records, which we cross-checked for exclusion errors against 115 studies from the PEI
State of Economic Inclusion Report evidence database (Andrews et al., 2021). After removing duplica-
tions, the search produced 2,604 unique candidate records. We then applied an initial relevance screen,
retaining 306 semi-finalist studies for detailed eligibility review. The large difference between these two
steps is due to the search terms (especially ”graduation”) picking up many studies on education that
are not relevant to poverty graduation programs. We then assessed whether each intervention satisfied
our graduation program definition of including at least three of five core components: a lump-sum
transfer, a stream of smaller transfers for consumption support, savings support, curriculum-based
training, and coaching or follow-up support. 4
Specifically, each study we include meets the following criteria:
1. The study is a randomized controlled trial.
2. The comparison arm received no intervention, a placebo, or business-as-usual services (such as
small regular transfers for consumption support).
3. The intervention was administered in a low- or middle-income country (as defined by World Bank
classification in August 2025).
At the level of the treatment arm, we use the following inclusion criteria:
1. The treatment arm administered at least three of the following five eligible treatment components:
(a) Consumption support
(b) Savings support (access or encouragement)
(c) Asset or lump sum cash transfer
(d) Skills training
(e) Coaching
2. The study reports results on any of the following outcomes: consumption, income, assets, employ-
ment, savings, food security, mental health, life satisfaction, aspirations, or female empowerment.
3Specifically, a June 2024 EconLit search used("graduation" OR "livelihood" OR "multifacet*") AND
("randomized" AND "evaluation") AND ("poverty" OR "low income") NOT "teacher", with related terms and all
years enabled.
4In September 2026, we added 8 studies that had been issued since our initial search and met the search criteria,
with the objective of ensuring that the results remained up to date.
4
Our inclusion criteria imply that we focus on multifaceted graduation and economic inclusion
interventions. We do not include simple “cash-plus” programs that administer a cash transfer and
only one additional treatment component (such as training). We note that some recent government-
led programs layer multifaceted interventions on top of public works programs. In this case, workfare
replaces regular cash transfers for consumption support. We do not include these programs unless they
independently meet the three-component criterion. This is because the number of studies is limited at
the time of writing, and public works imply different types of labor shifts and opportunity costs than
regular consumption support.
2.2 Sample Description
The final analysis sample draws on 49 study records from 41 publications, reports, and working pa-
pers, covering 40 unique randomizations. Across these records, we observe 81 reported treatment
variations and 123 treatment-variation-wave observations; consolidating repeated reports of the same
intervention lineage yields 68 unique treatment arms and 109 canonical treatment-arm-wave observa-
tions. Figure 1 summarizes the final analysis sample. 5 Our sample includes programs evaluated in
26 countries. Coverage is concentrated in Sub-Saharan Africa, but it spans South Asia, Southeast
Asia, Latin America, and the Middle East. About a quarter of the studies occurred in fragile or post-
conflict settings (specifically: Afghanistan, Burkina Faso, Chad, the Democratic Republic of Congo,
Niger, South Sudan, Uganda (with refugees from the DRC), and the Republic of Yemen).
Appendix Table A.1 reports component support and outcome sample sizes. In terms of compo-
nents, all treatment arms include training, and a majority includes an asset or lump-sum transfer,
coaching, and/or savings support. Despite these high-level similarities, the component details vary
across treatment arms. The value of lump-sum transfers varies sharply across treatment arms: some
variants omit a productive transfer entirely, while others provide transfers worth more than USD 1,000
in 2020 PPP terms (Data Appendix Table 2). Program cost and duration also vary meaningfully
throughout the sample. Income, consumption, and assets are all reported for a majority of treatment
arms, with coverage falling sharply for other outcomes, as we discuss next.
2.3 Data Extraction
2.3.1 DEVIDENCE Ecosystem for Data Extraction and Quality Control
We extracted treatment effects from published papers and appendices using the DEVIDENCE ex-
traction workflow from the Global Poverty Research lab at Northwestern University. For each study,
the extraction instrument recorded study metadata, publication and appendix links, treatment-control
comparisons, survey waves, units of randomization and analysis, treatment and control sample sizes,
treatment components, outcome labels, units, transformations, baseline values, endline values, and
5Data Appendix Table 1 lists all the included studies and references. Data Appendix Table 2 provides details on the
program components for each unique treatment arm.
5
reported treatment-effect estimates. We use reported estimates rather than re-estimating effects from
microdata.
When multiple estimates were available, we prioritized estimates that were disaggregated by treat-
ment arm and survey round. Within each arm-wave cell, we selected the measure with the highest
control group mean when there were multiple measures of monetary and non-index outcomes; for
indexed or standardized outcomes, we used the broadest measure possible. For example, the highest-
control-mean selection criterion led us to prioritize total household consumption over food consumption
alone and total household income over income from a single activity.
2.3.2 Key Outcome V ariables
We report 12 outcomes grouped into consumption, income, food security, savings, assets, employment,
psychological well-being, and female empowerment.
Consumption
Monthly household consumptioncaptures household-level consumption or total expenditure. If not
available at the household level, we scale per-capita consumption linearly by household size. If total
consumption is not available, we use the consumption or expenditure category with the next-largest
control group mean.
Income
Monthly household incomecaptures household-level income or earnings, and total revenue for busi-
nesses. Similarly to consumption, if household-level measures are not available, we proxy by per-capita
income adjusted for household size. If no aggregate measure of total income is available, we use the
income, earnings, or category with the next-largest control group mean.
F ood Security
Food securitycaptures study-reported food security scores, indices, and related indicators, coded so
that higher values indicate greater food security. The included studies use both established instruments—
including the Food Consumption Score (FCS), Food Insecurity Experience Scale (FIES), Household
Food Insecurity Access Scale (HFIAS), and Household Hunger Scale (HHS)—and author-designed in-
dices based on experiences such as insufficient food, meal skipping, reduced portions, or going an entire
day without eating. We prioritize author-reported standardized indices where available and harmonize
the direction of all included measures.
Savings
Savings stockprioritizes savings balances or stocks where available. When no stock measure is re-
ported, we use savings flows, such as deposits over the month preceding follow-up.
6
Non-Financial Assets
Total assetspicks up measures of the total stock of household assets. If not available, we use the asset
category with the next-largest control group mean.
Employment
Any work reportedcaptures whether households report any form of work. We use this as the reported
employment outcome because activity type and work-intensity measures are less comparable across
studies. We note that studies do not consistently report engagement across all forms of work (in ei-
ther wage or self-employment, on or off-farm).Self-employment/Business operationcaptures whether
households report self-employment in off-farm income-generating activities or business operation.
Psychological W ell-Being
Mental healthcaptures mental health and psychological well-being indices, such as the Kessler mental
health score. If no standard index is reported, we use author-designed scores. In the absence of any
general index, we prioritize depression scores and indices. If none of the above are available, we use
single mental health symptoms or perceived stress scores. In 6 of the 18 studies contributing to the
mental health outcome, the selected measure is a narrower symptom, stress, or psychological-distress
scale rather than a broad mental health index.Satisfaction and happinesscomprises simple, one-item
life satisfaction and perceived happiness measures.Aspirations and expectationsis comprised mostly
of measures of general, educational, or child-related aspirations or general measures of future expec-
tations. If neither is available, we proxy with measures of optimism and whether respondents expect
life to improve. In three studies contributing to aspirations and expectations, the selected measure is
a proxy based on optimism, hopelessness, or whether respondents expect life to improve.
Empowerment
To capture notions of women’s empowerment, we use agency and general empowerment indices.
Agencyis a measure of household-level decision-making power and mostly picks up on indices about
women’s say in resource allocation. If no index is reported, we proxy by simple one-item measures
of power in household resource allocation and decision-making.General empowermentis strictly a
measure of general women’s or partner’s empowerment or disempowerment indices.
2.4 Costs Data
Of the 68 unique treatment arms in our sample, 48 provide intervention cost estimates, which for
descriptive reporting we express in constant 2020 market-exchange-rate USD per household, using
reported nominal costs where available and PPP-backconverted nominal equivalents otherwise.6 Across
these 48 arms in Data Appendix Table 3, estimated costs range from 102 USD to 3,090 USD per
6The quality of cost data varies widely, with some papers mentioning a unit cost without providing detailed informa-
tion and others providing detailed cost breakdowns.
7
participating household. The median cost is 445 USD, and the mean is 819 USD. One notable pattern
is that several of the higher-cost programs and pilots were designed before 2016.7 Government adoption
of graduation programs increased over time and accelerated after 2016, and programs with government
involvement tend to have lower costs when they leverage national social protection systems.
Partly due to the varying cost reporting standards, we estimate parallel cost models with the
same observable program characteristics: a nominal model for funder-facing cost reporting and a
PPP model for analyses that compare costs directly with PPP treatment effects. Among the 38
canonical treatment-arm observations used to estimate the nominal unit-cost model, the covariates
explain substantial within-sample variation in costs (adjustedR 2 = 0.41, see Appendix Table A.2).
Given the selected sample of programs reporting costs, we use the models for prediction rather than
interpreting individual coefficients causally. The cost-effectiveness analyses below use predictions from
the PPP model so that costs and treatment effects share the same basis; reported PPP costs remain
the denominator in the benefit-cost analysis.
3 Methodology

heterogeneity from sampling variation, describing how impacts vary with program composition, and
deriving persistence and cost-benefit estimates from uncertain impacts. These challenges are partic-
ularly important when investigating graduation programs that differ across settings,
